summary: Solid, multiply-sourced, family-friendly core exists. The tunkuluchu (also spelled tunkuruchu) is a Yucatec Maya name for a night owl (tecolote / buho). Its call heard at night is a folk omen: people say that when the tunkuluchu sings, someone will die, so villagers feel fear when they hear it. The best-known origin legend: the owl was once the wisest, calmest bird; it was invited to a party of the birds, drank balche and got dizzy, a mocking man teased it (pulled its feathers, pricked its feet) while the other birds laughed; ashamed, it vowed revenge, spent nights in the cemetery learning to recognise the smell of death, and now sings near people who are about to die. Soften the death element for a beginner story (say bad news / someone will leave us / a sad thing) and hedge that it is only what people say.
facts: The tunkuluchu (also tunkuruchu, tunkuluchuj) is a Yucatec Maya word for an owl; Barrera Vasquez's Diccionario Maya Cordemex (1980), as cited by Kettunen 2016, glosses tunkuluchu as 'buho' / 'lechuza' / 'especie de lechuza' and tunkuruchu as 'tecolote o buho'.

It is a general owl name, not one fixed species: EcuRed says tecolote/tunkuluchu is a common name in Mexico, El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras for several small owls of the family Strigidae; the Spanish word tecolote comes from Nahuatl tecolotl (EcuRed, es.wikipedia).
It is a nocturnal bird of prey; the tellings place it alone among ruins and wandering cemeteries at night (EcuRed; Vocal retelling).

Folk meaning: its call is an omen; the saying is 'when the tunkuluchu sings, a man (someone) dies'. Stated in EcuRed, Yucatan Today (Cantarell), Cultura Colectiva, De Peso Yucatan, tucuentofavorito and Vocal tellings.

Villagers react with fear: EcuRed and the Vocal retelling say the Maya tremble when they hear the call because everyone knows what it announces; Pata de Huech says even the bravest feel it, and some people trust a talisman to protect them.

Best-known origin legend (party version), consistent core across EcuRed, Yucatan Today (Violeta H. Cantarell), Cultura Colectiva, De Peso Yucatan, tucuentofavorito and Vocal: the owl was the wisest, prudent, quiet bird of the bird kingdom, others sought its advice; it was invited to a royal/palace party of the birds (it rarely went to parties); it drank balche, a Maya drink, and got tipsy; a man at the party (called annoying/bully/mocking in different tellings) pulled out its feathers and pricked its feet with a thorn; the birds laughed; ashamed, the owl swore revenge; it went to the cemetery night after night to train its sense of smell until it could recognise the smell of death; ever since, it perches near people who are about to die and sings, which frightens people.

Short alternative explanations recorded by EcuRed and the Vocal retelling: some say the owl sings out of spite, others because it enjoys walking among cemeteries on dark nights, and some say a Maya sorceress (bruja) turned into the owl after she died.

Dual reputation: Diario de Yucatan (2022; only the intro is visible, rest paywalled) calls the tunkuluchu the Maya 'messenger bird', linked in Yucatan folklore both with wisdom and prosperity and with death and misfortune. EcuRed and the legend itself also keep the idea that it was originally the wisest bird.

The omen belief fits a wider Maya-area pattern. Kettunen (Jagiellonian Univ. / Univ. of Helsinki, Contributions in New World Archaeology 10, 2016) concludes that owls are mostly considered bad omens and harbingers of death in the Maya area, with some ambiguity (e.g. a good sign for hunters in other Maya groups).

Yucatec dictionary glosses collected by Kettunen from Barrera Vasquez 1980: xoch' / xooch' = 'lechuza, ave nocturna, agüero de los indios' (a night bird that is an omen); ikim / ikin = 'una de las aves agoreras que temen los indios' (an omen bird the people fear); kuy = 'lechuza, ave agorera' (also in Chilam Balam texts); buh = 'tecolote o buho'; t'oojka' x nuuk = small pygmy owl. So Yucatec has several owl words and several are explicitly glossed as omen birds.
Balche is both a tree (Lonchocarpus longistylus, native to the Yucatan Peninsula, sacred to the Maya) and a ritual alcoholic drink made by fermenting its bark (Gobierno del Estado de Yucatan).
Mayab is used in the tellings as the setting: the land of the Maya (Yucatan peninsula) where the lone owl lives among the ruins (EcuRed, Vocal, Yucatan Today).

The Yucatan state government's 2025 Festival de las Aves Toh press note says a puppet show told Maya legends of the Pajaro Toh, the Tunkuluchu and the Choms, showing the tunkuluchu legend is still told to families and children today (it gives no text of the legend).

Popular scientific note given by one explanatory page (todosloshechos.es, no cited source): owls call to talk to other owls, not to announce human deaths; Jorge Moreno (De Peso Yucatan) likewise says owls are not evil and their bad name is undeserved. Useful as a gentle closing line.
variants: A. Party/balche revenge version (the most common, 'consistent core'): wise owl -> invited to birds' party -> drinks balche -> a man pulls feathers and pricks feet, birds laugh -> owl vows revenge -> learns the smell of death in cemeteries -> sings near people about to die. Details differ: who the man is (annoying Maya man / bully / young Maya man who is also drunk / just 'a man'), whether the owl is the revenge target of one man or of all humans, whether the party is in a royal palace, and whether the owl dances/jokes (EcuRed, Cultura Colectiva, tucuentofavorito) or is just handled roughly (Yucatan Today).

B. Revenge aim differs: Cultura Colectiva and Lifeder-type tellings say the owl wanted to warn the mocking man of his own death; EcuRed, Yucatan Today, De Peso Yucatan and tucuentofavorito say it turned against people in general (frightening anyone who hears it).

C. Witch/sorceress version (EcuRed, Vocal; Pata de Huech): a Maya witch who died became the owl, or the bird is a witch in bird shape; Pata de Huech also calls it a priest who attends the dying and says it can be tamed, which no other source says.

D. Wise-counsellor / peacock-king version (Yucatan Today 'The Owl, Wise Counsellor', Manzanillo Sun 2019, Lifeder): the owl advises a peacock king, is forced to attend and dance at a banquet, is mocked, hides, tries to read a sacred book to expose the king but cannot read in the daylight, and the gods punish him so he is seen only at night. It explains why the owl is nocturnal, is not a death omen story, and is weakly sourced; use only as a separate tale, not mixed in.

E. Dual meaning (Diario de Yucatan): messenger bird linked with wisdom/prosperity as well as death/misfortune. Elsewhere in Mexico owl omen sayings exist (such as 'when the tecolote sings, someone dies') but are general, not specific to the Yucatec tunkuluchu.

F. Skeptic/modern voice: Jorge Moreno (De Peso Yucatan) and todosloshechos.es say owls are harmless birds with an undeserved reputation; Pata de Huech claims the death-bird idea was a Spanish invention to keep people indoors at night (single blog, unverified).

maya_terms.meaning: Yucatec Maya name for an owl, the night bird of the legend; popular spellings vary (tunkuluchu / tunkuruchu are both widely used, with or without accent on the last syllable). Glossed 'buho' / 'lechuza' / 'tecolote o buho' in Barrera Vasquez (1980) via Kettunen 2016. Possibly an imitation of the owl's call, but this is unverified (Kettunen says it could be onomatopoeic or part of a wider Maya owl-name family).
sacred tree of the Maya (Lonchocarpus longistylus) and the ritual fermented drink made from its bark; the drink that makes the owl dizzy at the party.
the land of the Maya, the Yucatan peninsula, where the owl lives in the tellings.
Yucatec word for barn owl / lechuza, a night bird that is an omen (agüero) for the people (Barrera Vasquez 1980 via Kettunen 2016).
Yucatec lechuza / omen bird that the people fear (Barrera Vasquez 1980 via Kettunen 2016).
Yucatec onomatopoeic word for a 'tecolote o buho' (owl) (Barrera Vasquez 1980 via Kettunen 2016); buj is the Itzaj and Mopan form.
Yucatec 'lechuza, ave agorera' (omen owl), also in Chilam Balam texts (via Kettunen 2016).
Spanish word for owl in Mexico, from Nahuatl tecolotl.
the Maya underworld (K'iche' / Popol Vuh term); only for background, not part of the Yucatec village legend.

cautions: DEATH OMEN is sensitive: for a beginner family story keep it light and hedged ('people say...'), e.g. 'when the tunkuluchu sings, people feel sad news is near'. Do not say the owl causes death; the legend says it only senses and announces it. Do not describe the dying or cemeteries in detail; a short mention of the cemetery is fine (the owl 'learned the smell of sadness') or leave it out.

Do NOT use the saying 'cuando el tecolote canta, el indio muere' (it is a general Mexican saying and uses an offensive/colonial term); also skip the claim that it was invented by the Spanish (single blog, unverified).

Alcohol: balche is a ritual alcoholic drink and the owl gets drunk in the standard telling. For a children's or beginner story, say the owl 'drank a strong sweet drink and felt dizzy' or just 'the owl was tired and dizzy at the noisy party'; avoid 'drunk'. Keep the word balche only if you add that it is a special Maya drink.

Violence/teasing: keep the humiliation mild (a man teased the owl and pulled a feather; the birds laughed). Do not include the thorn pricking if you want it gentler. The 'man' is described as an annoying/bully/Maya man in different tellings; call him 'a rude guest' to avoid ethnic stereotyping.

The popular tellings (Yucatan Today, EcuRed, Cultura Colectiva, Vocal, tucuentofavorito, De Peso Yucatan) are not independent: they share one core text and most cite no oral informant, so we have few sourced village-level accounts. The legend is 'commonly told' but not fieldwork-documented in what I could access.

Yucatec-specific ethnographic proof of the omen is only indirect: the strongest source I could read is Kettunen 2016 (dictionary glosses of xoch', ikim, kuy as omen birds and a Maya-area summary). Reports attributing the omen to Chan Kom (Redfield and Villa Rojas 1934), Brinton 1883 and Landa came to me only via a secondary search summary of a 'Maya Gods of War' chapter whose page I could not open; verify before citing them.

Species is not settled: tunkuluchu is a general owl word. One search-tool summary of the CICY 'Guia de aves de Xocen' said the name Tunk'uluchu' / Tunk'uruchuj is used there for the Great Horned Owl (Bubo virginianus); I could not open the PDF (too large) and no second source confirms it. Do not name a species in the story; say 'a small night owl'. Also the apostrophe spellings (Tunk'uluchu') are unconfirmed; use tunkuluchu / tunkuruchu.
Etymology (onomatopoeia) is unconfirmed; Kettunen only says it may be imitative or related to a wider family of Maya owl names. Do not claim 'its name sounds like its song' as fact in the story.

The Yucatan Today 'Owl, Wise Counsellor' / Manzanillo Sun / Lifeder peacock-king version is a different tale, is inconsistent (it calls both the peacock and the owl Tunkuluchu), says Puhuy is a 'woodland turkey' (a Por Esto legend says pujuy/puhuy is a nocturnal roadside bird, tapacaminos, who lent feathers to the peacock) and mentions the Popol Vuh (a K'iche' book, not Yucatec). Do not mix it into the party-revenge story.

Do not import K'iche' / highland material (Popol Vuh owl messengers of Xibalba, tukur) into a Yucatec village story; it is a different Maya region and language. Xibalba is not needed for a beginner story.
Pata de Huech claims (bird can be tamed like a dog, is a priest of the dying, hunts bats and does not eat carrion) rest on one blog author; do not use them as facts.
Religion: avoid presenting owl beliefs as what 'all Maya believe today'. Phrase as 'in some villages people say' or 'old stories say'. Mention that many people today simply enjoy owls as birds.
suggested_story_core: In the Mayab forest lived a wise little owl, the tunkuluchu.
The birds invited him to a big party, and he drank a sweet drink and felt dizzy.
A rude guest teased him and the other birds laughed, so the owl felt very ashamed.
He decided to learn the secrets of the night and went to the quiet places by himself.
Now, in the old stories of the village, when you hear the tunkuluchu sing at night, people say sad news is near.
A moral some retellings draw: hurting someone's pride can turn a kind friend into a sad one (todosloshechos.es).
But the owl is just a night bird that likes the dark.
